explanation: His father Daedalus made the wings to escape Crete and warned him to fly neither too low nor too high. Phaethon also fell from the sky, after losing control of the Sun's chariot.

claims.text: In Greek myth, Icarus flew too close to the Sun on wings of feathers and wax, and the wax melted.
Daedalus survived the flight, Phaethon drove the chariot of the Sun and Perseus flew on winged sandals, so none of them is the boy whose wax wings melted.
Daedalus made the wings so that he and Icarus could escape from Crete.
Daedalus warned Icarus to fly neither too low nor too high.
In Greek myth, Phaethon fell from the sky after losing control of the chariot of the Sun.

evidence.restatement: Icarus flew too near the Sun on his father's wings of feathers and wax; the wax melted and he fell into the sea.
Daedalus reached safety, Phaethon drove the chariot of Helios, and Perseus flew on the winged sandals; none is the boy whose wings melted.
Daedalus made the wings so that he and Icarus could escape King Minos's Crete.
In Ovid's telling Daedalus tells Icarus to keep a middle course: too low and the sea's damp weighs the feathers, too high and the Sun melts the wax.
Phaethon lost control of the Sun's chariot and was struck down from the sky by Zeus.
Icarus, the son of Daedalus, flew on wings of feathers and wax and fell when the Sun melted the wax (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8).
Daedalus completed the escape, Phaethon drove the Sun god's chariot with no wings, and Perseus used winged sandals; only Icarus is the boy of the wax wings.
Held on Crete by King Minos, Daedalus built the wings so that he and his son could leave the island.
In Ovid, Daedalus tells Icarus to take the middle course, not skimming the waves and not climbing towards the Sun.
Phaethon lost control of the Sun chariot and Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt.
